value.overview: The Slaty-backed Forest-Falcon is a secretive forest raptor of the family Falconidae. It spends much of its time in dense tropical vegetation, where its slate-gray back and quiet, low-level hunting style can make it difficult to detect. The species has a broad but discontinuous distribution in Central and South America. It is generally uncommon and localized, especially where mature forest has been reduced, but it remains distributed across a large global range.
value.classification: The Slaty-backed Forest-Falcon belongs to the falcon family, Falconidae, and the forest-falcon genus Micrastur. Its scientific name is Micrastur mirandollei.
value.identification: This medium-sized forest-falcon has mainly slate-gray upperparts, pale underparts, a dark tail with narrow pale barring and a whitish tip, and yellowish facial skin, legs, and feet. Its shape is compact, with relatively short, rounded wings and a long tail suited to maneuvering through forest. Juveniles are browner above and more buff or scaly below. The species is more often detected by its distinctive loud, repeated nasal calls than by prolonged views.
value.rangeHabitat: The Slaty-backed Forest-Falcon occurs from Costa Rica and Panama through western Colombia to western Ecuador, with a separate extensive population in the Amazon Basin and adjacent regions. In Costa Rica it is a resident of the Caribbean lowlands, especially from the San Carlos and Tortuguero regions southward toward Panama. It favors humid lowland evergreen forest, particularly mature and relatively undisturbed stands, but may use mature secondary forest and areas near streams. Most records are from low elevations, generally below about 500 meters.
value.migrationStatus: It is considered a year-round resident, including in Costa Rica. There is no reliable evidence of regular long-distance migration or predictable seasonal passage.
value.breeding: The breeding biology of the Slaty-backed Forest-Falcon is poorly documented. Available references provide little dependable information on courtship, nesting dates, clutch size, incubation, or parental care. As with other Micrastur forest-falcons, it is generally believed to nest in natural cavities in trees, but this species-specific assumption should be treated cautiously until more observations are available. In Costa Rica, breeding is expected to occur within its permanent lowland forest range.
value.dietFeeding: Its diet includes small birds, lizards, and snakes. It hunts mainly from the forest understory and lower to middle levels of the canopy, using concealed perches and short, rapid pursuits through vegetation. It may also descend to the ground. Like some other forest-falcons, it may take advantage of prey flushed by army-ant swarms, although the importance of this behavior for the species is not well established.
value.behavior: This forest-falcon is usually solitary, quiet, and difficult to observe. It moves through dense forest with quick, agile flight and often remains hidden on shaded perches. Its repeated nasal calls may carry farther than the bird can be seen and can stimulate mobbing by smaller birds. It is most likely to be detected by careful listening in suitable lowland forest rather than by searching open skies.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is believed to be decreasing, but the size and direction of regional populations, including the Costa Rican population, are not well quantified.
